title: Exclusive Interview with Luke Floriea
text: Welcome back to Cleveland Browns Daily, brought to you by Bally Bet, official sports betting partner of your Cleveland Browns. And very happy now to be joined by the hometown hero, Luke Floria. Luke, try to put into words if you can, your life journey and what it meant to catch a touchdown in Huntington Bank Field wearing a Cleveland Browns uniform. >> Yeah, so uh grew up huge Browns fan, grew up in Mentor, so 30 minutes east and uh go to all the games. My dad has season tickets for forever, so me and him would go to all the games together. I've been seen a lot of good games, seen a lot of bad games, everything in between and uh you know, catching that first one was special. It was a dream come true. You know, you you kind of like dream about it as a kid growing up, but you really never think it's actually going to happen and then it happens, so yeah, it was really special. >> So, you think go back to last year, we go to Carolina, you catch the big ball down the sideline and it's like all the Floria-Dorian connection, it's there. And then unfortunately, you got injured on that play and then we didn't get to see you again. Now, you go to Chicago, there it is again, right down the field, Dorian to Luke Floria. And then we get into this game and you catch the touchdown. When you did suffer that injury, did you think that this was still possible? >> Um yeah, I think you have to. If you don't want to get in that mindset where oh, I'm out of it or whatever, that's the only way to get really through that injury and get through last season and uh you know, keep working hard, keep my motivation so I can get in opportunities like that and have moments like that that uh mean a lot to me. It's a really a blessing every time. >> All right, pre-snap on that play, did you think you were getting the ball? Like once it was called, were you like oh, this is this is good. >> I knew I had a shot. We threw it earlier in practice that week. We ran the same play and I got it and I was like, okay, hopefully it's the same coverage and then ran my dig, turned the corner, and I'm like, oh I'm wide open. >> Yeah, a little bit of a bust, which is good. >> worked out well. >> Yeah, so when he throws it, was it like slow motion to you? >> Yeah, well, those are the hard ones actually. When it's coming in like that, you're like, oh shoot, you got a lot of time to think about it, but make sure my feet were in everything, but yeah, I mean, it was cool. >> So, it was cool watching it. The guys right behind you went absolutely nuts who were there. And obviously, I'm sure you got Did you have a lot of family there? >> I did have a lot of family and friends there. >> Okay, so let's take me from okay, we celebrate. Did you look for them anywhere? >> They're on the opposite side of the stadium. I knew I knew where they were at, so. >> So, what talk me through post game when you finally get to see your family and your friends? >> They were excited. That My dad was probably the most excited, I think, out of anybody. You know my dad, you know he's never like that. But it was really special for Yeah, so it was really special for my whole family. You know, I had a lot of friends there. I got a million texts from everybody, which I always appreciate, so it was really cool. >> It was a very cool moment. And then what I like too is one of the things I always look for when we're up in the booth and you know, calling the games, how do your peers respond? >> Yeah. >> And they were fired up for you. >> [laughter] >> Like that's that's when you know you've earned their respect and they have a a great affection for you. >> I I love all the guys here. Our receiver room is great. The new guys that just came in, the rookies are awesome. The vets that have been in the league for a while that are here, they're all great. We have a really great room and the coaching staff's awesome. So yeah, we all get along well. We're all like brothers, so yeah, it's awesome. >> It's a young room. I mean, it really is. You're talking about Jerry and Tyler and I Malachi is probably considered a veteran in that room, but it's a young room. Is that fun to have a bunch of guys of a similar age together? >> I do think it's a great mix, you know. >> Judy and Tyler and the Anx and then got all the young guys with Casey and Denzel and Cole and all those guys. It's a really great mix in that room. >> So, you worked hard to get back. It feels like as we've gone through this camp, we're seeing your opportunities increase. We're seeing you get some some run with the ones as well. Kind of how has that process been for you and and how would you evaluate how things have gone for you? >> I think things have gone well. You know, I just I tell everybody I take it day by day. I take it play by play. I don't read too much into one play or one rep or anything. I'm just going to go out there. I'm going to give everything I have for that one play, then off to the next one. >> Do you like this offense? >> I like this offense. I scored I scored my first touchdown in it. I can't complain about [laughter] it too much. >> What do you like about it? It does I mean listen, there's tons of 11 personnel. There's tons of three by ones. There are tons of cool concepts and it seems to be very much geared towards the pass and wide receivers. >> I just think there's a lot of versatility and you know, you can catch screen passes, you can get jet sweeps, you can get the ball long down the field, you can get short ones that are right to you and easy and you can move the ball that way. So I I just think the versatility in this offense is great. >> You got one more opportunity in the preseason Thursday night against the Patriots. National TV prime time. You're well known in this area obviously coming out of Mentor. Now you got a chance for the national audience to get to see you. What do you hope to to put on tape on Thursday? >> I just hope to put good football plays on tape like I hope I've been doing so far leading up to this point. You know, I want to go out there. I want to A lot of people have never seen me play, don't know anything about me. So I want to put my best stuff on tape so they think, "Oh, 81's not bad." >> Yeah, right. Exactly. Who are some of the people that you like to watch past or present? >> So you guys have Julian Edelman, obviously Kent State guy. I have to >> Say him first. Wes Welker. >> Wes Welker. >> Patriot. I had a feeling we were going this direction. >> Kind of kind of Patriot. I'll go other Patriot, Doug Baldwin, older guy from Seattle. I love Cole Beasley, Dallas Clark while I love. Um my favorite receiver growing up actually I have saw him I think they had a preseason game it was like early 2000s maybe. Terrell Owens. I was wearing a Browns I was wearing a Browns jersey but I actually had a Terrell Owens jersey on underneath. He was my favorite player at the time. >> So was that 49ers T.O., Cowboys T.O., Eagles T.O., Cowboys T.O.? Okay. All right. Big dude. >> Physical guy. What do you like about him? >> His touchdown celebrations. I was like 7 years old. It was awesome to see him dance in the end zone. >> So one day if you score in Dallas, are you going to go run to the star? >> I don't think so. I don't think [laughter] I got that in me. >> I remember that well then Roy Williams came out of nowhere and blasted him and Ndamukong Suh did it. I think that's wise. What's it been like having a head coach and the guy who's really running this offense, coordinating this offense, calling plays, Todd Monken, who is a receiver guru at heart. I mean, he's a quarterback guru, but he's a receiver guru. He is very hands-on. He is very particular with you guys. What's that been like? >> It's been awesome. You know, he's never going to let a rep slide, even when we're just doing routes on air. If you're off by a foot on where your landmark's supposed to be or whatever, he's going to let you know about it. But I think it's great for our development and then hopefully the team's development. Just him being there all the time. You can tell he's a little bit harder on the receivers than a lot of other spots, which I I like and I think all the guys can appreciate. >> Well, the receivers have had a lot of success under him at everywhere he's been, every level. So, it's a thing that he knows a little bit about >> that. >> Yeah, exactly. And I think that's one of the things you see some of the offenses that have a lot of success in the league. They are You have the details matter, the techniques matter, every little thing matters. Is that probably one of the things you've noticed kind of going from Kent State to the NFL is just that it's it's the margins that determine everything. >> Yeah, you run a good route in college, you're open by 5-6 yards. You run a good route in the NFL, you still might not even be open. You're open by a yard and you're considered wide open. So, that's really the main difference, I would say. >> What do you think has been your chemistry with Shedeur? I mean, it's just been apparent since last year to this year. Why is it Why has that worked? >> Honestly, I don't really have an explanation for it. We've gotten a lot closer on and off the field. Obviously, spending the last year together. It was really since we came in for rookie mini camp. He was the first person I met when I walked in the door. We ate lunch together. We got to know each other a little bit. Then he was just like, "Hey, rookie mini camp comes, I'm going to feed you." I'm like, "I appreciate it. Thank you." So, just kind of been that way ever since. >> Yeah, listen, quarterbacks like guys who are open and you catch it. >> I I think so, too. >> That's right. That makes you a quarterback's best friend. >> Do you like the fact that there are so many things that you can do from the inside of formations? Obviously, not to label say you're a slot receiver only, but this is an offense that provides, as you talked about earlier, so much variety for guys lining up on the inside, a variety of splits. Some of them will be condensed formations, some are, you know, wider formations, but you really can run the entire route tree from the inside. >> Yeah, you can. That's as I said, another perk of the offense with the versatility. You know, some plays I'll line up in the same exact spot and I'll run an in and next play I can run an out and next play I can run by and next play I can shut it down and run a hitch or a stop or whatever. And that's the thing, keeps the defense guessing, keeps the DBs guessing. They can never really jump routes or guess cuz if they do, they could be completely wrong and bust and give up a big play. >> Whenever you guys are in the ones where you're you've got somebody outside of you, you're inside of them. So either two's on that side or the three by one when we're near that, and you run either a wheel, I don't know if you guys call it a wheel or kind of like a slot fade. It's always coming to you. >> It's money. >> Yeah, it's money. >> It's one of my favorite plays we have. >> Yeah, that one [laughter] seems like an automatic. That's an automatic. >> Doesn't it get a little rub off that, too? It's not It's It's a nice concept that coach Monken drew up. >> Yeah, it is a good concept. Well, Luke, it's great talking with you. Congrats on getting that touchdown. Excited to see more. What would it mean to you to make this 53-man roster? >> Uh mean everything. I mean, it's a dream come true to be in the position I am now and now it just kind of make it even greater. So, uh working for it. Uh whatever happens happens, but I'm excited to be a Cleveland Brown. >> Well, we're all rooting for you, Luke. Awesome story. Great job out there. Let's get some more touchdowns at Huntington Bank Field in prime time. >> Absolutely. >> All right. We'll be back with more Cleveland Browns Daily brought to you by Bally Bet right after this.

Uh 10 and five Trey. Um they're unbelievable, man. unbelievable people, unbelievable persons. Uh, for me, man, it's been a true blessing to be able to have like two guys like that. Like two vets. I mean, yeah, I would say they're vets. Um, but they're I mean, I don't want to call them old, but they're not that old, but like I mean, they've been in the league for a while now. Um, so like be able to have guys like that and guys are just really good individuals and willing to help me out when I ask questions. um be willing to just talk outside of football, just being a guy, just being a brother. I mean my football knowledge has grown a ton and I feel like that's the sense of the football knowledge has helped me out on the field. Um I think from a standard of footwork I think uh the attention to detail that coach day does uh I think it's an amazing job and I've spent a lot of hours working with coach day on stuff um just inside the building in the film room on the field and for me I couldn't have asked for a better quarterback coach. Uh, Coach Day is a guy that teaches and coaches and is a true teacher of men and does an unbelievable job teaching offense and also coaching. Um, and he doesn't he doesn't really care if you're the first string guy or the third string guy, he coaches everybody exactly the same. And that's something that uh I feel like I got lucky with. text: All right, good morning. >> Jaylen's done a good job of bouncing back, getting back into the swing of things, just continue to get reps to, you know, build up his stamina to get out there. I don't think anybody really knows that, but I feel like you get really good reps with your wounds in joint practices. Um a little bit of experience um and a little bit of understanding for for this offense. Um, you know, there's a lot of off the- field stuff that goes into it that, you know, wasn't expressly told to me, but, you know, we we took Marlin with one of the second round picks. What does it look like to approach whenever that would, you know, be the first time that we think it would make the most sense for him to impact and influence positive change with us. I mean, that I I I I I don't even understand it. It's true. I mean, I'm looking at this stuff. I'm like, surely that's not real. I I think that's a never-ending journey of becoming, right, Maria? But uh what I do like is I love the way that our guys are working, you know? I think we're building skills. And so, I've been really pleased with that. I love the collective character of this group. I love how we're coming together. I like some of the depth that we've been able to form because of some of the guys that are absent and so, I'm really enjoying it. Um one of those guys will be the backup in Australia, but you know, we're going to have three quarterbacks on this team that are going to be, you know, good football players and I think those guys have done a really good job. >> What is the value to having a running back like Ronnie Rivers who can do so many different things? >> Yeah, it's huge, Nate. He's got a good feel in the screen game. Um you know, Ronnie Rivers is the guy that uh you know, you you're very appreciative of and you know, we got two great running backs in Kyren and Blake that, you know, are going to be building on what they've done. Uh but if for whatever reason, you know, they need to be supplemented, you know, Ronnie Rivers is the guy that I trust. >> When it comes to special teams, >> I'll come back to you. >> you're playing some offense and defense and guys, >> Yep. What's the balance between kind of splitting that up best out of them in those two >> It's a great question. I think it's a feel. You know, I think how many of the action plays, you know, the one thing that's really been a big change is is the impact of the kickoff and the kickoff return phase. Just with the uptick of analytics and how people approach it. So, it's a significant impact. The punt phase is something that is, you know, is so vital and so important. That's where you see a lot out our key players that are starters on both phases there. Um but I think it's a feel. I think but what is important is, you know, how important that phase is and how impactful that is. Think you've seen some of the investments and I think it's more really important to be able to subconsciously communicate without necessarily it's not the words it's seen is better than said. Um you know, with some of the coaching things with the way that see a lot of different guys involved and then how we try to make it important whether it's in the team meetings, in the special teams meetings. And so that'll be an ongoing thing but that's a big area of improvement for us because I'm not going to run away that I haven't done a good enough job of making that an emphasis and um and it's cost us and that's nobody's fault but my own. Yep. Yeah, that'll be the case. Yep. All right. Thanks, guys.

So he's always talking to me like obviously now because it's practice he's able to talk whenever in the mic during the play he's saying stuff in there but obviously I know on Sundays he's not going to be able to but he's always giving little reminders to tell tell this guy this tell this guy that just to make sure everybody's on the same page. So that's why uh for me as the one of the leaders of the defense I take pride in being able to you know carry that communication straight from the coach and give everything that I need to say to the other guys. How much of what? Sorry. How much of what he says to you is a play call and how much of it is like a tip or whatever? >> He'll say the play call one time, maybe twice. Everything else is all tips. Look at this formation. Tell them the down and distance. Especially now he's walking me through it since I'm new to it. So, he's giving me, you know, all the keys to keys to success with it. Tell them the down a distance. Tell them the situation. If it's two-minute, tell them this, this, and that. if it's fourth down or third down, tell them like what they're we're expecting to see. So, I think he's doing a really good job of teaching me like how a typical green dot would do it, especially in not being a linebackers. Sometimes I have to talk to the Dline and it's something that I've probably never had a conversation about about the fronts or a blitz pattern or anything. So, I have to be able to learn those things myself to be able to so it's not, you know, it's not some random words that I'm just spitting out from coach. It's something I can understand, too. I was going to say, is there has there been any time where he's been like, "Wait, I I don't know what you just said." >> Sometimes, but now that I I've gotten a hold of it, I'm like, "Okay, now I need to learn every single part of the defense." So, if I hear because you can't hear every single word coach says, especially imagine it being third down, home game, crowd is loud. You'll have to hear one word and that can be your trigger word to know the exact call or know what coach is trying to say and get that point across. So, I think even more so, we already are, but me and Lou have to get on a super like I got to be thinking how exactly how he's thinking and I think we got a good head start on that um last year and now obviously going into this season, our second year in the system, I'm able to hear one word of the call and know exactly what it is and narrow it down of what I'm expecting him to call in certain times. >> Can you explain because it's sound like a lot, but you only got a certain amount of time to do, >> right? So, can you explain what a game day like for general fan like play call comes in? How much time you got? Like what does that look like? >> You have about 5 seconds to really get in the huddle, hear the call, and you may or may not hear it fully. So, you you're almost playing telephone for me. I walk when I when I wasn't the green dot. I'd walk next to the linebacker like on the bottom of the huddle, not where I'm back with the DBs behind. I'd walk to the side so I can hear it clearly. Then I'll walk and tell the corner nickel and the other corner and the other safety just to make sure we're all on the same page. So um the communication like within the cycle of a snap you depending on what the play was before imagine it's a catch tackle you got to jog back offense has what 40 seconds um to get back and and snap the ball. So by the time you get the call in they line up you only have about 15 seconds left and then the play the clock from when Lou can communicate with the green dot is at 15 seconds. So you have to get those few seconds of communication. Then the whole all 11 guys has to be on the same page. So there's a lot that goes on within the cycle of a snap. And I think it's really playing telephone and trusting that this guy got the call so he can tell me the right call also. >> Is he in your ear? I mean as soon as the 46 starts is he? >> Yes, for sure. >> So >> regroup and then >> No, that's part that's part of it. like I have to be able to critique my last play myself, digest what I saw from the offense, but I'm also hearing the next play call, hearing him say the situation cuz he's he's really good coordinator when it comes to when I'm jogging back, he's giving me, okay, what to expect here. It's second down and short, expect a shot, they're in shot territory. Certain things that he's able to mention there that I have to put in my mind just so I know, okay, I can tell this to my DBs after I get the play call out. Play call is always number one. So that's the number one thing you have to listen out for. But everything else you can tell the specific guys. If it's a DB thing, I'm not going to tell the Dline what specific to the DBs and vice versa. >> And 15 seconds is off. >> It's all communication. >> It's all it's all up to you. Now >> if you're in the middle of saying something, >> that's why you just got to that's why I mentioned you have to know the buzz the buzzwords of if it's the front, you know, this front is always accompanied with this call. And when you know the defense and you know I know Lou well well enough to where I can expect what he's calling on third down. So if I get a certain front and it's third third down to seven, I know these few calls that he'll have on every third and seven. So I think it's also my job to be able to be super close with Lou knowing what to expect from him. So I think we got a good head start on that last year. Me just getting closer to him and us having our meetings every Friday or Saturday just going over the game plan. And I think that's something that will continue this year so I can know exactly how he's thinking. >> We've seen it throughout camp. >> Yeah, just being somebody that's accomplished so much um and still very intentional on how he practices, how he communicates out there. So, I think um obviously the accolades carry a lot of weight, but it's more than just just the accompl accomplishments that he's made um on the field. He's a leader off the field when it comes to talking to the younger guys, coaching something up, warning the young guys during a preseason game. Simple things like that. Him being a good teammate, standing up during a preseason game, coaching up the DBs when they come to the sideline, telling them what to expect. I think that's something that you may may or may not get from a superstar like him. But ever since day one, he's come in and has been really intentional with it. And I think the people follow just because obviously we all know everybody's known who Sauce was ever since he got into the league and had a lot of respect for him, the what he's done in the league, but coming here and being as intentional as he is and practicing hard and, you know, being a good good leader and a good voice in our DB room. >> Last one here. >> Feel I guess your career was involved with it. you feel now a handful of years into it, your body needs a preseason like to to play in the game? >> Um, I would say no. I would just because you said need. I don't think we need it, but it's never it's always the the battle of, you know, it'll never hurt you. Um, obviously unless you're physically hurt, we pray that never happens and it's football at the end of the day. But I feel like when you get to a certain age, you've had so many reps under your belt to where if I was if it was week one tomorrow and we had to go play Baltimore, I'd be ready just off of the reps I've gotten, uh, the mental preparation, physical preparation. I think everything we've done in our career after a certain point, you can, it's like riding a bike. But obviously, like I said, it won't hurt because reps are reps and game reps are different than practice reps where you're tagging up, getting full tackling. I think tackling is always the biggest thing when it comes to getting used to for the season. So, I think it is productive to play in the preseason, but I wouldn't say I wouldn't say you need it. So, I think that's the key word. You don't need it, but it's always productive for sure. >> So, coach says, "Do you want to play Saturday?" >> We're rolling. >> Yes. Yeah. >> All right. Couple games under your belt. So, what was it like to you all this prep going into the draft and you got to run before you do whatever and play and actually have takes to kind of face your game. >> Uh it definitely feel good to go out there on the field and play. You know, it's it's always a great feeling to put that helmet on and strap up, put the pads on to go out there and compete. So that's my probably that was my biggest thing from last time just, you know, just getting transition from that combine and all the jumps and just getting back into my playbook and getting ready to play some ball. So that was that was big for me. I know we talked um after you drafted about how much of your college experience was just transitioning from um new position position now that you've been integrated into um an NFL franchise onto the offseason work on training camp. Um where do you feel like your game has evolved most? I'll probably say just getting better at the little things, you know, just just uh you know, detailing my well looking at the film and detailing going off that, you know, just getting with my coaches, seeing what I could do better, just being more intentional with like the little things I could do better as far as footwork and hand placement and stuff like that. I'll say, >> George, having a few different joint practices and multiple preseason games, where have you benefited differently from each of those experiences? Uh, I feel like I probably benefited just like getting different looks. You know, it's not like in college where you get where you go against your teammates the whole offseason, then your first different look would be your first week one. So, I just feel like the joint practice was good for me because, you know, I just got a good got a chance to get go against different tackles, you know, see myself against different talents and different like skill sets. So, I feel like that was the biggest thing for me. >> George, with um this week being last week across the league, you anticipated an intense week of practice and the games as well on Saturday with everyone who's planning to be on >> Yeah, you know, well, I beg your pardon one more time. >> Yeah, sorry. Uh, do you anticipate it being an intense week of practice in the game with roster cuts coming this weekend and everybody wanting to be on that final? >> Yeah, no doubt. I feel like it would be a definitely a good intense practice, good intense week for, you know, this upcoming game. You know, everybody scratching for that 53 53 man roster. So, I definitely agree with that. So like you guys are all >> but in practice when it's like oneonone reps versus individual offensive line versus like 11 on 11 play >> do you have like a different mentality in those like are you working on craft specifically in one >> uh the way I kind of approach oneon ones is like it's it's like you said it's very different you know you know you in game play you you're going to you It's a fourman rush or fiveman rush against their five or whatever protection they have. But you know when I the way I approach 101's I just try to win in my own ways like whether that being inside or outside. But I definitely try to focus on some of my craft. I go into every wester like I try to have a plan you know okay I want to hit this whether it's going to be a speed move or power base. But, you know, me personally, I'm more of like I like like ingame rushes or like, you know, five on four or like cuz it kind of feel better like, you know, you don't know like, okay, I took the inside, but I don't get my D tackle. He didn't uh he didn't watch me. So, the quarterback is out. So, that's that's a bad rip on me. So, I feel I feel like rushing like as a unit is better for me. >> You went against obviously your teammates for a little while and you had a few practices >> against your teammates. Were you just kind of some of those blockers and Falcons and Patriots kind of just playing the hits what you're good at or how that >> Yeah, I Yeah, I'll probably say like the starter camp I it was just learning like okay who does what. But like at the same time I'm more of a I like to play aggressive. So like be myself to make them force their hand instead [clears throat] of like watching what they're doing more so. And then like once we get to the joint practices, it's probably just like you said, just throwing your best hitter. Like what what I feel most comfortable with, what what I feel like I'm going to win with, that's what I'm going to throw. >> If if five years ago somebody had said you're going to be an NFL defensive end, what would you have told? >> Five years ago, uh I was like what, freshman, sophomore year of college? Yeah. I was I was still a walk-on. So I was still a walk-on at Northern Illinois. So, I'll be like, "Kudos to me." Cuz right now, [laughter] right now, right now, we still trying to work up that depth chart. I'm probably like the seven, eight man on the tight end. Yeah. So, it'll definitely be a shocker for hearing that. [laughter] >> All right. Thanks, >> Justin. One thing we're talking about Kevin was asking him about it the other day. Your ability to play through the entire catch. Where do you think that comes from and how much of an emphasis is that in your game? We saw it like Drake practice where like it looked like a catch probably for two seconds and then that last break it out. >> Um really started in college when I was in college we really emphasized on finishing the play through the hands. No, we worked on it kind of every day. I was joking with the guys about it. They I was like when I was in college, we literally did that drill every single day and really emphasized and it kind of carried over now that you know the play is never over to the ball to the players on the ground or the balls on the ground. So I just try my best to finish every play like that. >> This is Shane's kind of using this to simulate a game week um with this practice schedule and everything leading up to Saturday. What do you want to get out of it as somebody who's never been through that in the NFL before? >> Um really just understanding of how the week goes from week to week. You know, like this at this time last year I was kind of out of it. It's kind of uncharted territory for me. So, I think it's really good to get a practice run at it before, you know, week one comes around and get on the field. >> Was that Wisconsin game? Was that the last game you played? >> Yes, sir. Almost two years. >> Is it I guess how much you look forward to Saturday? >> Can you repeat one more time? >> How much are you looking forward to Saturday? I mean, it's been nearly two years. Just playing a little bit. >> I'm looking forward to it a I mean, I kind of want to play the whole preseason, but I finally get a chance to get on the field and like I'm blessed, you know, like I ain't been on the field in a long time and to be on the biggest stage and get a chance to play, it's a blessing and just can't wait for it. >> You started out camp playing slot and then, you know, moving out last week, you're playing outside a lot. How's the How does that help you? How do you play both positions in this defense even though you haven't played the game yet? >> Um, really just gain an understanding of the whole defense. Like when you're in slot, it's a whole different world than being outside. But I know the coaches really done a really good job. And over this past year when I was out, I kind of did a good job of understanding both positions a lot. So when I'm in there at corn, I know what I'm doing. And it's kind of seamless just to bump inside and play inside. >> Is is it Which one's easier outside because you can get your hands on them a little quicker or >> they both come with a different set of challenges. I wouldn't say one's easier than the other one. It's kind of when you're outside you a lot more covering a lot of different receivers you'll see out there and inside you know it's a lot more you run fit you got to know a lot more you got to communicate a lot more so it's just different worlds and you know when you understand defense you got to learn how to balance both of them >> we were talking to Cam about how he's wearing the green dot calling defense what makes him a good communicator how he kind of I guess got behind him as the green guy >> well before he had the green dot he was the one talking the most on on the field so now he has it you know for us it was kind of like we're comfortable with it because he always was the voice and now in the huddle he's the guy you know giving out the calls and stuff. So it helps us a lot cuz we were kind of used to him being the voice of the secondary for last year too. Justin, returning to game action, what do you anticipate most? Whether it's about returning to play or just returning to entire game. >> Um, really everything, the entire experience. I ain't played in a minute. So, just to be under the lights, be in front of a full crowd, you know, get going on the field with your brothers, you know, going full speed, full at it, I think it's going to be pretty fun. Kim was telling us earlier this afternoon about what Sardner is like said that he's really intentional about working with guys on the field off the field especially in this training camp process. What has your experience been like working with him and how has he helped you grow as a >> I think one thing he does really well is communication like in walkthroughs he's always talking talking through routes uh formations and he's really intentional about things he do. There's never a play where he just takes off and just does his own thing. He kind of holds on to the details. And when you have a allp pro guy that does the small things, right? The younger guys like like me look up to him and like see what what it takes to be all pro and why he's so special in this league. >> What did you know about him before he joined back in? >> I didn't really know much. I kind of knew he was a really good player, but as a person, I didn't know anything about him, but being around him every day, you kind of get to understand his personality. He's a real good guy to be around. All right. >> All right. Thank you guys. >> What has it um what's it kind of been like um trying to get up to speed while you know miss some practice and all that, but I mean have you tried to have you had to do extra stuff on on the side and meetings and what have you. How have you tried to kind of stay stay up to speed? I guess >> Oh, I mean no doubt. I mean I think everything around here is film as far as like the walk through and the practices. So, just making sure like, hey, I'm honing in on that, you know, even though I'm not actually in taking the rep, but watching the guys in front of me that took that rep, you know, I might get that same rep or just knowing trying to know what what I do. >> Now there's been a few days. How how do you look back at your experience on Saturday? >> I mean, it it was good being out there playing football. I mean, anytime I know for me, like I know I missed a lot of time, man. So, anytime I'm out there playing football, man, it's and strapping my helmet up, man, it's it's a blessing. So, man, it felt good being out there. What things did you look at and say, "Okay, all right. This is where I did all this to improve." >> I think just overall just the the game, you know, just playing football, man. I think you always can get better at that, man. It's nothing that you can uh you can say, "Hey, I did perfect, man. It's always room to improve." >> Is it is it frustrating knowing that, you know, just having to sit out a couple weeks has kind of maybe put you in a rotation where you know like you're probably going to be starting the game, >> man. Well, if I was starting like what? It don't matter how that situation might look, man. I'm still going to show up the the the same way and work hard and control what I can control. I don't look at it like that, man. I just, like I said, control what I can control. Show up to work. >> We were talking to Cam about him wearing the green dot. What makes him a good communicator in your eyes? >> I think he's just always talking. you know, he's uh you can you can you know when Cam is back there talking and stuff and just getting guys on the same page and overcommunicating. >> You and Bryce alternated with Jaylen game for a while. What was feedback like between I guess both? Well, just stay on top of our keys, knowing what to expect, uh different formation, this different alignments and like personnel, knowing when this certain tight ends right here, uh he might go back and how deep he is. So, stay on our keys just stuff that we uh go through on the on the linebacker room daily. >> I'm sure that's that's unique, but being the preseason and not being that experience kind of like Yeah, for sure. You definitely can say that, you know, getting that out, you know, getting that in your system, getting that under your belt. So, anytime you get to scrap it up against someone else, it's always good. Anyone >> else? >> Thank you. I appreciate you.

title: Minnesota Vikings Team Press Conferences | August 25 | 2026 Training Camp
text: You've seen everything before. How How's your training camp different than all that you go through when you've been through one before? >> We'll just say like from beginning to now, it's like last year we're swimming. I was like I was trying to figure out what was going on, the tempo of which things were were going on. Um kind of uh the switch between periods, trying to get my my brain switched up depending on the periods where you're going on, what plays were happening. Now, it's more of just a understand the language, understanding of the picture of what's going on, the tempo of what's going on, um and be able to um you know, adjust a little easier, I think, between periods and be able to to really be in the moment. I think last year was hard to really be grounded. I think because I've done it for a year, um it's a little easier to be in the be in the moment, be grounded. >> Is that what it's like in a game, too? Does it slow down a little bit every game? >> I would I believe so. I think that going into a huddle, too, uh that's that's part of how you can kind of judge yourself is how do you feel walking into the huddle? Um and being really honest with yourself. And walking into the huddle, you know, so far has been has been great. And uh you feel on the in the in the guys, too. The The guys feel the same energy when you walk in. And when everyone kind of feels that collective positive energy, um and confident energy, um then it typically you know, turns out successful for the team. >> Knowing what you know now, what's the most difficult part of being an NFL quarterback? >> Oh, man. I would say the entire job is difficult. Um you know, I I honestly, I would say I would say that uh having an uh an internal confidence over like an external confidence, I think, is is something that that changes from like college to the NFL. I think you you become um as a quarterback in the NFL, um there can be a group of either four guys, three guys, two guys on a roster depending on what it is. And everyone's Everyone is expected to compete at the highest level, no matter if you're a starter or if you're the third or fourth string. Um and to be to be able to go on the field and have the same success, um and lead the guys the same way, um that's a really challenging thing. We don't get a ton of reps. And going from college to being the starter to the NFL where you're not always a starter, um that is the most challenging thing. And I think having a a of guys around you that understand that, having coaches that understand that, um guys that are willing to stay after practice with you and and work those reps mentally and physically. Um that's where people can get better um and that's where I found I can get better is continuing to get those reps mentally and physically during and after practice. >> So, the D-line has been having a one heck of a camp. Yourself in particular as well. What have you liked so far that's really worked for you? >> Uh really just me and being able to be locked in and buying every day. You know, we've been playing a new position, you know, new things for me. Just me being able to execute new things every day step by step. >> What does B Flo tell you when he talks to you one-on-one? >> He just tells me to keep going, you know, with all the new things that's on my plate considering that I'm playing edge and a little bit more on third down this year, you know, just being able to stay grounded and be willing to learn every day. >> And edge too, it seems to bring out the fun side of you. That's what it seems like when you're on there. What do you like about that? >> It's a little bit more space. You can have a little bit more freedom, you know, um it's it's it's a lot it's a lot of fun. >> And you work with guys like Levi, also uh Jaylen, young guys that are really finding their way in this D-line. What have they meant to you? >> It's kind of hard not to like those guys, you know, we have a lot of fun off the field, but most importantly, you know, they're always willing to help me on the field, you know, my first year last year they was able to give me a lot of tips, you know, help me learn a lot. So, being able to be in a room with those guys is is nothing more nothing more than I would want. >> And now talking with uh Dallas Turner, we talked about being on the edge. It's his strength that he really worked on this year coming into camp. What is the mindset shift for you? So, not the physicality, the mindset that you've had to work on. >> Just um the mindset just being able to be relentless, you know, um in every every alignment that you play in. You may be aligned on the tight end or a tackle, you know, just being able to you know, defeat the block with whoever's in front of you. >> [laughter] >> What what can you say about a guy like Miles so far like >> Miles is definitely a special person. You know, he's different. He's probably the funniest guy on the team to me. And he come to work every day, you know, I think Miles has had a big camp and a great preseason. >> And finally, going into the final preseason game, I know that there's some guys in the team might have jitters with the 30th coming up or whatnot. What What do you kind of mindset-wise going into this final game? Everyone wants to stay healthy, wants to hit their cues, but what are you thinking? >> Just put your best game forward, you know, have no doubts, and play your best game, and play as hard as you can. That's all I can say.

You know, just doing everything I can to be able to get back as soon as possible. >> What were some of the things you picked up about the defense just being on the sideline? >> I think just watching us play like I like our style of play. Like we've been real physical out there. I obviously know there's little things we got to clean up on like our technique. Just making sure we're all on the same page like our communication could be a little bit better but the style of play has been there. That's been a good thing for sure. Urge. >> What did you like about what the defense did today? >> I think today we just strained. You know, we're like in the the end of the dog days of camp. Nobody's feeling good. Everybody's dealing with something. So just being able to come out here consistently just keep straining. I think that was a good thing. Now we've just got to be able to just pick up on the details. Be consistent. >> I know nobody's more frustrated about dealing with what you've had to deal with from an injury standpoint. >> Uh >> First few years of your career than than you are. Has it been particularly frustrating last couple weeks with obviously starting job open? Has it been stressful? >> I mean it is tough but I've been there before. I think for me just trying to just minimize them. You know, last week I or two weeks ago I had like a little sub tissue things like scar tissue so I'm just taking care of that. Be able to come back as quick as possible. And yeah, it is frustrating but I mean what's for me is for me so just continue to stay positive, have a positive mentality and just attack it when it come back around for me. >> How do you feel like you and Chris Johnson could potentially compliment each other as a duo? >> I think we compliment each other real well. All the guys as well. Me, J. Marsh, Marco, A.J., whoever may be but speaking of Chris specifically, I think he's a little bit more of a a compact type of defender and I'm a longer guy but I have some of those same tangibles. Just what have you seen from his growth the past couple weeks? >> Simply, I would just say he's a competitor. I like that. He just come out and compete every single day. It ain't always be pretty. Um he's a competitor. Um I think he does do a good job of just being keen on his details. Um right? Like using his right techniques at the right time. That's a big thing, but first come first, he's just a competitor. So, that's a big thing. It's courage. >> Just one more health question. Anything still lingering from the November injury against the Commanders, or do you feel totally back? >> No, I feel good. Yeah, that was, you know, I had a little ankle. Um but the ankle feels good. Now it's just me just minimizing the football stuff, soft tissues and all that. We not here in Miami. title: Offensive Coordinator Bobby Slowik meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: First, what were your thoughts on Malik at the joint, and then his first preseason game? >> Yeah, it's really been the same message since the beginning. You know, he's been a really fun guy to be around, really fun guy to work with. He's been awesome in the building, he's been great on the field, and he's just consistently gotten better uh in everything that we're doing. And and really, you know, there's a lot that goes along with the quarterback position. You got to handle yourself, you got to handle the huddle, you got to handle the the guys around you, you got to make sure that you're on your stuff, you got to make sure they're on their stuff, you got to help guys out uh post-huddle. Like, there's there's just a lot of things that naturally come with the position that he handles with ease, really. Um so, that's been pretty awesome to see. And and just to see his continued improvement every day within what we're doing has been fun. >> Bobby, looking back at the Giants joint practice, and I I know it's been a little bit, but when you you reviewed the film, what did you notice relative to why the Giants had too many pressures? >> Yeah, I'm really, we just we weren't on our assignments, you know what I mean? Which has kind of been a thing. I think as you go through camp, we have probably what's going to wind up being one of the younger offensive rosters in the NFL. Um and and just the consistency of our assignments as a starting point is definitely something that we we got to continue to improve upon. You know, like, we're well aware we got a long way to go. Um and it starts with just doing our job first. And then within that, making sure our technique's right, our fundamentals are right. Um you know, that that practice was fun. There was a lot of back and forth. We actually hit a lot of runs. Like, our run game was was pretty solid in the joint practice, but the pass game, particularly the protections, we know that that can't happen. So, we're on the road to fixing it. >> How would you assess the quality of play by Proctor throughout camp? >> Yeah, it's Yeah, really same as Malik. You know, he's only had limited game action so far, but um you know, you kind of take into consideration the joint practice, you take into into consideration all the stuff we've done against our defense, and he's taking steady steps, like all our young guys. Like, they're steady steps. There's stuff that he has like there's a reason we took him in the first round and it shows, you know? Like we're really excited about the the talent he has. Um but just continuing to hone in on the consistency for all these guys is going to be is is is going to be really on us as coaches. Like we really got to do a good job developing uh and and really letting these guys go play fast and having that consistency is part of what they're doing. >> Bobby, with Chris Bell, how do you envision using him when he gets fully healthy? Could he be a guy that throws those quick hitters to him and gets you some run after yards catch? >> Yeah, I mean obviously he's only practiced a a little bit here and there, but uh just going off his college tape, like some of the things that were awesome to just watch him do, like he's a he's a really big dude, he's a really fast dude. Uh he's hit some wild numbers on GPS considering his size. He's got great hands. Uh he's a tough tackle. So, I mean you could do a lot of things with that as far as a receiver goes. He's a good ball in hand player. He's a good guy that can make competitive catches. He can go down the field uh and he can run underneath routes. So, I I think the more we get used to just being with him, we'll kind of settle into what exactly his role is going to be for us. Um but from his college tape, there's there's not many limiting factors as far as what we're going to let him at least explore. >> And from seeing Kevin Hogan back the past week, what skills do you like about him? Do you think he can help you early this season? >> Yeah, I mean he's he's really fast, you know? I think that's obvious to everybody. Like he has a he has a different gear in speed. Um many he made some really nice plays in that last game. Like he he's a big competitor. Like really shows up in competitive situations. I think that kind of jumps off. Um now I'm going to be saying the same thing really for a lot of the young guys. Like we got to get the consistency going in what we're doing to make sure that we can go do our job and just execute as an offense, but he's been exciting to work with and to and to have out there and make plays. >> Bobby, sort of a macro question when it comes to coaching the quarterback. We have a big arm quarterback like Malik. Does it change the way you teach anticipation because he can't see and think out there or is it all the same uniform >> No, it's I would say like never in coaching is anything uniform. You know what I mean? And that that's not just quarterback play. I'd say that's really every position. You know, like Devon's going to be different than Ali. He's going to be different than Jay Wright. Um Dulcich is going to be different than Kasmerek. You know, like you can go down the line. Like you got to make sure you're using what your guys strengths are. Um I would say with Malik, he has no issue throwing with anticipation. He has no issue throwing on time. Uh he also has no issue if he has to go off schedule, make someone miss and extend the play. So there's there's a lot of tools at his disposal. And right now it's more like we we got to get on the same page with our receivers. We got to get on the same page with our tight ends. We got to we just got to do our jobs better. We got to coach better. >> Given that Quinn is going through an injury or two, does that affect how you evaluate his performances or do you have to take it at face value what he's giving you right now? >> I think there's a lot of different factors that kind of play into the whole evaluation thing. Like all from our perspective as far as coaching goes, like really you're so in the moment every day. All you're trying to do is for every individual like incrementally get them better at every moment. And it's been hard with Quinn the last week or so not being able to be out there, you know. So he's been doing everything he can in the meeting rooms. He's been trying to take another step mentally as far as our scheme and what he's doing, but um it was nice having him back out there today. Obviously a a little limited in what he could do, but he was out there and and letting it fly when he could. Um and you know, we'll see where it goes from there. >> Bobby, as it relates to your eligible receivers, wide wide receivers, tight ends, running backs, would it be a bad thing if Devon Achane was the leading receiver this season? >> Uh not if we had a whole lot of yards, you know. Like I think that the way we kind of approach all this is you just want to have an efficient offense. [snorts] You want to have a productive offense. And how you distribute targets within that, like you're always going to make sure you lean on guys' strengths. You're going to lean on things that that guys can do that are different than other guys. Um but the way you disperse those targets is just where do you think you can attack a defense with your personnel? How can you protect yourself against issues that come up as you do that? And then um from that point on it's it it really kind of the chips fall as they may. >> It's been reported I'm sorry Bobby. It's been reported that uh Atlanta is going to play its starters and possibly game plan. Will that affect your approach on Friday? >> No. No, our approach is generally the same. The preseason for us is very much an evaluation process. So um ours doesn't change that much. >> You all signed four veteran receivers obviously with Jalen Tolbert, Jalen Reagor, Quez Watkins, Tutu Atwell, Terrace Marshall. Who of those four Bobby do you think has been the most consistent of those four? >> Yeah, that's that's uh I I think really all four of them have had different moments, you know? You go through camp like camp's so long. You know, it's it's at what moment are we talking about who cuz everybody has ups and downs. It's the same as during the season. Everybody has ups and downs. Like Tutu, I know he had a he had a drop in the last game. Um but he he really before that game had shown up in the last couple practices. You really could see his speed. You could feel his competitiveness. He was getting open even when he wasn't getting the ball. T Marsh has been a factor in the run game like every time he's on the field he's impacting the run game which has helped us immensely. Uh JT obviously is is taking a like his probably dip was early on in camp and he has really rebounded strong from that. He's been doing a really good job lately as as far as, you know, how he's going about his job, how he's helping the young guys, how he's approaching the game. So like you could go down the line of our whole receiving crew. And really all of them at different moments have done really positive things and things they know they need to improve upon. So, we just got to keep shoring up the weaknesses. >> How because the run blocking and run game been both with starters and reserves? >> I think it's been good. I think the run game really for us in camp is largely been one of the highlights of what we've been doing. You know, it's it's something we want to emphasize. It's something Half wants to emphasize. I believe in running the ball. Our O line is well equipped to run the ball. Um you know, and I think when we've gone through camp and we've done things that we anticipate doing as we go through the year. Like we we really have done a good job creating windows and holes and our backs have done a good job seeing it. So, we're pretty confident. >> Couple more guys? >> What's impressed you specifically in the run game? I mean, physicality or short runs, short yardage, first downs, anything you can >> Yeah, I'd I'd I'd say probably the the versatility of what our personnel allows us to do. You know, you got my man who who and and Proctor on the left side that just and there's massive humans on the left side that can still move really well. So, you can get on the perimeter, you can get on the edge, you can also do stuff that's more duo-ish up the middle, you can do inside zone, you can do stuff with Malik in the run game. Um obviously, Vaughn has speed to get to the edge. He can hit it up in the middle as well on on the right side. Um you know, I think Jonah's really done a good job this camp as far as adjusting to right guard and how he's been progressing. Austin's been great to see step in there and create movement and work together with Jonah to build a rapport. Brew is Brew. You know, he's one of one of my favorite guys to watch practice. Um and then the probably the biggest thing for us in the run game that I think we do that not everyone in the NFL does and our guys right now have have done a really good job with it is is our tight ends. Like our tight ends have really embraced the run game. They've taken a step in how we want to approach the run game and it's all it's a lot of new faces. You know, the only guy who was here was Greg. Um and there's there's a little bit of a learning curve, but now that they've been rolling in it like you can feel their impact on the edge of defenses as well. >> Final question? >> I think I saw Malik Willis address the offense at one point during practice. I'm not sure if you saw the same thing or if I saw it right. Do you like that? >> Yeah. Yeah, you always want your quarterback to be a leader. You want your leaders to always take command and control, especially when you want them to take control all the time, but when you're going through a moment of adversity, today wasn't necessarily the best offensive practice. Um and you know, we kind of had to get it going there. So, you always want to rely on your leaders to do that.

Of course, the Jets have a lot of targets. I thought it was fascinating that Reich said that I look at this starting unit and said and and say and can say that, hey, listen, we got 15 guys.
